title: This isn't just a Visualiser, it is a Superpower
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that most teaching advice is too complex, and that four simple, relentlessly applied routines do most of the work: cold call as often as possible, put student work under the visualiser, choose work at random, and use a timer for every activity. His test is that students then work hard, think hard and remember more. He supports the claim with a head of science's follow-up email after a one-hour coaching session, describing a photosynthesis lesson rebuilt around cold calling, turn and talk, visualiser feedback on a six-mark question and a timer. She reports students initially nervous but then enjoying the tension, scores rising from 2-4 to 4-6 marks, and a lesson that was easier to prepare. The evidence is one teacher's report rather than data, but it shows his case that simplicity beats complexity.
points: Complex teaching solutions have many ways to go wrong, while simple ones are close to foolproof and so more powerful.
Four routines, cold calling, visualiser, random selection and timers, are meant to be applied relentlessly rather than decorated with nuance.
The goal behind the routines is that students work hard, think hard and remember more, independent of any inspection.
A teacher's follow-up shows bouncing questions between pupils and checking work on the visualiser generating feedback and measurable improvement on exam questions.
The changes also made the lesson easier to prepare and more enjoyable to teach, which supports adoption.
quotes: Complexity is my enemy. Complex solutions have multiple ways of going wrong. Simple solutions are almost foolproof.
I could give you 6-10 bullet points to exemplify the nuances of each one. 40 layers of complexity.
I never do anything just for Ofsted. If students work hard, think hard and remember more, they’ll be sorted for life, even if Ofsted disappears.
If pupils did not know the answer the questions was bounced to another pupil then back to that same pupil. I repeated some questions to check they were listening.
At first they were very nervous about answering, but then got into this and even said they enjoyed it as one pupils said they “enjoyed the tension”. Their knowledge and understanding did improve.
But also importantly this was an easy lesson for me to deliver and to prepare. It now makes me want to change a lot of our current resources!

I was on a roll today and used Mini whiteboards to quiz year 9 on key concepts this afternoon instead of doing a copy and complete in the book! I could see easily who knew what and when I could move on to the topic.
